subject: Anatomy
topic: Lateral Medullary Syndrome Wallenberg Vascular Territory
stem: A 62-year-old man presents with sudden-onset severe vertigo, nausea, and unsteady gait. Neurological examination reveals: loss of pain and temperature sensation over the left side of his face and the right side of his body (arms, trunk, and legs); left-sided ptosis and miosis (left Horner syndrome); left-sided limb ataxia with dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing; and severe dysphagia, hoarseness, and loss of the left gag reflex with the uvula deviating to the right. Muscle strength is 5/5 bilaterally, and light touch and vibration sensations are intact throughout. An acute ischemic infarction in which of the following arterial territories is responsible for this clinical presentation?

options.text: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) supplying the dorsolateral medulla
options.explanation: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome) is caused by occlusion of the POSTERIOR INFERIOR CEREBELLAR ARTERY (PICA) or vertebral artery. Key localized structures: (1) NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS (CN IX, X, XI motor) -> dysphagia, hoarseness, loss of gag reflex, uvula deviation away from lesion (pathognomonic); (2) SPINAL TRIGEMINAL NUCLEUS and tract -> ipsilateral loss of facial pain and temperature; (3) SPINOTHALAMIC TRACT -> contralateral loss of body pain and temperature; (4) INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE -> ipsilateral limb ataxia; (5) DESCENDING SYMPATHETIC TRACT -> ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis); and (6) VESTIBULAR NUCLEI -> vertigo, nystagmus. Pyramidal corticospinal tracts and medial lemniscus are medial and therefore SPARED.

options.text: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) supplying the lateral pontine tegmentum
options.explanation: AICA occlusion causes lateral pontine syndrome, which features ipsilateral facial motor droop (CN VII nucleus) and sensorineural hearing loss (CN VIII), absent here.

options.text: Paramedian branches of the basilar artery supplying the medial pons
options.explanation: Paramedian basilar branches supply the medial pons; occlusion causes contralateral hemiparesis and abducens palsy (Millard-Gubler), not lateral medullary Horner and nucleus ambiguus dysphagia.

options.text: Anterior spinal artery (ASA) supplying the paramedian ventral medulla
options.explanation: ASA occlusion causes medial medullary syndrome: contralateral hemiparesis (pyramid), contralateral loss of vibration/proprioception (medial lemniscus), and ipsilateral tongue deviation (CN XII).

options.text: Posterior cerebral artery (PCA) paramedian perforators supplying the cerebral peduncle
options.explanation: PCA occlusion of midbrain perforators causes Weber syndrome (ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral hemiparesis), not medullary Wallenberg syndrome.

explanation: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome) is caused by occlusion of the POSTERIOR INFERIOR CEREBELLAR ARTERY (PICA) or vertebral artery. Key localized structures: (1) NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS (CN IX, X, XI motor) -> dysphagia, hoarseness, loss of gag reflex, uvula deviation away from lesion (pathognomonic); (2) SPINAL TRIGEMINAL NUCLEUS and tract -> ipsilateral loss of facial pain and temperature; (3) SPINOTHALAMIC TRACT -> contralateral loss of body pain and temperature; (4) INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE -> ipsilateral limb ataxia; (5) DESCENDING SYMPATHETIC TRACT -> ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis); and (6) VESTIBULAR NUCLEI -> vertigo, nystagmus. Pyramidal corticospinal tracts and medial lemniscus are medial and therefore SPARED. Ipsilateral facial + contralateral body pain/temp loss + ipsilateral Horner + ataxia + dysphagia/hoarseness (CN IX/X) = Wallenberg syndrome -> PICA occlusion in lateral medulla.

Ipsilateral facial + contralateral body pain/temp loss + ipsilateral Horner + ataxia + dysphagia/hoarseness (CN IX/X) = Wallenberg syndrome -> PICA occlusion in lateral medulla.

subject: Anatomy
topic: Medial Medullary Syndrome Dejerine Localization
stem: A 70-year-old woman with chronic hypertension presents with acute-onset weakness of her right arm and leg and difficulty speaking. Neurological examination reveals: spastic hemiparesis of the right upper and lower extremities with hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response (positive Babinski sign); complete loss of vibration sense and two-point discrimination over the right arm, trunk, and leg with intact pain and temperature sensation; and weakness of the tongue, which deviates to the left when protruded. There is no facial weakness, dysphagia, or limb ataxia. An occlusion of which of the following arteries is responsible for this patient's deficits?

options.text: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) supplying the dorsolateral medulla
options.explanation: PICA occlusion causes lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg) with dysphagia, Horner syndrome, and crossed pain/temperature loss, sparing motor strength and vibration.

options.text: Anterior spinal artery (ASA) or paramedian branches of the vertebral artery supplying the ventromedial medulla
options.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine syndrome) is caused by infarction of the anterior spinal artery (ASA) or vertebral artery paramedian branches. The syndrome is defined by a triad of structures localized to the ventromedial medulla: (1) CORTICOSPINAL TRACT in the medullary pyramid -> contralateral spastic hemiparesis (right-sided weakness); (2) MEDIAL LEMNISCUS (dorsal column fibers after internal arcuate decussation) -> contralateral loss of proprioception and vibration sense (right-sided); and (3) HYPOGLOSSAL NERVE / NUCLEUS (CN XII) -> ipsilateral flaccid paralysis of the tongue, which deviates TOWARD the side of the lesion (left) due to unopposed action of the contralateral genioglossus.

options.text: Superior cerebellar artery (SCA) supplying the rostral dorsolateral pons
options.explanation: SCA occlusion causes severe ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, Horner syndrome, and contralateral body pain/temperature loss, without tongue deviation or hemiparesis.

options.text: Anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplying the parasagittal motor cortex
options.explanation: ACA occlusion causes contralateral leg weakness greater than arm weakness and urinary incontinence, without tongue atrophy or selective medial lemniscal loss.

options.text: Lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery supplying the posterior limb of the internal capsule
options.explanation: Lenticulostriate infarction causes pure motor hemiparesis affecting face, arm, and leg equally, without tongue deviation or selective loss of vibration with intact pain/temp.

explanation: Medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine syndrome) is caused by infarction of the anterior spinal artery (ASA) or vertebral artery paramedian branches. The syndrome is defined by a triad of structures localized to the ventromedial medulla: (1) CORTICOSPINAL TRACT in the medullary pyramid -> contralateral spastic hemiparesis (right-sided weakness); (2) MEDIAL LEMNISCUS (dorsal column fibers after internal arcuate decussation) -> contralateral loss of proprioception and vibration sense (right-sided); and (3) HYPOGLOSSAL NERVE / NUCLEUS (CN XII) -> ipsilateral flaccid paralysis of the tongue, which deviates TOWARD the side of the lesion (left) due to unopposed action of the contralateral genioglossus. Contralateral hemiparesis + contralateral vibration/proprioception loss + ipsilateral tongue deviation = Medial medullary syndrome -> Anterior Spinal Artery (ASA).

keyPoints: Medial Medullary Syndrome Dejerine Localization
Contralateral hemiparesis + contralateral vibration/proprioception loss + ipsilateral tongue deviation = Medial medullary syndrome -> Anterior Spinal Artery (ASA).

subject: Anatomy
topic: Lateral Pontine Syndrome AICA Territory Deficits
stem: A 58-year-old man presents with sudden-onset vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and left-sided hearing loss. Physical examination demonstrates: complete paralysis of the muscles of facial expression on the left side, including inability to wrinkle the left forehead or close the left eye; absent left corneal reflex with normal right corneal sensation; sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear; severe left-sided limb ataxia; left-sided Horner syndrome (ptosis and miosis); and loss of pain and temperature sensation over the right arm, trunk, and leg. Muscle strength in all four limbs is 5/5, and vibration sensation is fully preserved bilaterally. Which of the following arteries is most likely occluded in this patient?

options.text: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)
options.explanation: PICA occlusion causes lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg); it affects the nucleus ambiguus (dysphagia/hoarseness), but SPARES the facial motor nucleus (no facial paralysis) and cochlear nuclei (no deafness).

options.text: Anterior spinal artery (ASA)
options.explanation: ASA occlusion causes medial medullary syndrome with contralateral hemiparesis and ipsilateral tongue deviation, not facial paralysis or deafness.

options.text: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA)
options.explanation: Lateral pontine syndrome is caused by occlusion of the ANTERIOR INFERIOR CEREBELLAR ARTERY (AICA). Key diagnostic structures localized to the caudal lateral pons include: (1) FACIAL MOTOR NUCLEUS (CN VII) -> ipsilateral complete peripheral facial droop including the forehead (distinguishing AICA from PICA); (2) COCHLEAR NUCLEI and internal auditory artery -> ipsilateral sensorineural deafness (pathognomonic for AICA); (3) VESTIBULAR NUCLEI -> vertigo and nystagmus; (4) SPINAL TRIGEMINAL NUCLEUS -> ipsilateral facial numbness; (5) SPINOTHALAMIC TRACT -> contralateral body pain/temperature loss; (6) MIDDLE CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE -> ipsilateral limb ataxia; and (7) DESCENDING SYMPATHETIC TRACT -> ipsilateral Horner syndrome. Corticospinal and medial lemniscus fibers are spared.

options.text: Labyrinthine artery alone
options.explanation: Isolated labyrinthine artery occlusion causes sudden deafness and vertigo, but does NOT cause facial paralysis, Horner syndrome, ataxia, or crossed spinothalamic sensory loss.

options.text: Middle cerebral artery (MCA) superior division
options.explanation: MCA superior division infarction causes contralateral spastic faciobrachial hemiparesis and Broca aphasia, sparing hearing, cerebellar coordination, and pain/temperature.

explanation: Lateral pontine syndrome is caused by occlusion of the ANTERIOR INFERIOR CEREBELLAR ARTERY (AICA). Corticospinal and medial lemniscus fibers are spared. Ipsilateral peripheral facial droop (forehead involved) + ipsilateral deafness + crossed pain/temp loss + ataxia = Lateral pontine syndrome -> AICA occlusion.

Ipsilateral peripheral facial droop (forehead involved) + ipsilateral deafness + crossed pain/temp loss + ataxia = Lateral pontine syndrome -> AICA occlusion.

subject: Pathology
topic: Ventral Pontine Infarction Locked-In Syndrome
stem: A 54-year-old man with uncontrolled hypertension and diabetes collapses suddenly. Upon emergency department arrival, he is completely unable to move any of his four extremities, speak, chew, swallow, or produce facial movements. He does not respond to painful stimuli on his body. However, when instructed to 'look up at the ceiling' or 'blink twice if you can hear me,' he reliably executes vertical saccadic eye movements and blinks voluntarily. Pupils are equal and reactive to light. Electroencephalography demonstrates a normal, reactive background waking alpha rhythm. Occlusion of which of the following vessels is responsible for this condition, and which anatomical structure is spared to allow vertical eye movements?

options.text: Anterior cerebral artery bilaterally causing extensive parasagittal frontal lobe infarction; sparing of the primary motor strip enables ocular vertical saccades
options.explanation: Bilateral ACA infarction causes akinetic mutism and abulia with paraplegia, but patients do not retain fully preserved cognition or isolated voluntary vertical blink communication.

options.text: Bilateral middle cerebral artery M1 segments causing massive hemispheric infarction; brainstem reflexes are preserved
options.explanation: Bilateral MCA infarctions cause fatal cerebral edema and coma, with loss of conscious wakefulness on EEG.

options.text: Vein of Galen thrombosis causing bilateral thalamic hemorrhagic infarction; sparing of the ventral striatum preserves blink reflexes
options.explanation: Vein of Galen thrombosis causes deep cerebral venous infarction with severe obtundation and coma, not conscious locked-in quadriplegia.

options.text: Basilar artery trunk causing extensive infarction of the ventral basis pontis; voluntary vertical eye movements and eyelid opening are spared because the rostral midbrain tectum, Edinger-Westphal nucleus, and oculomotor complex remain perfused
options.explanation: LOCKED-IN SYNDROME is caused by thrombosis of the basilar artery trunk producing massive bilateral infarction of the BASIS PONTIS (ventral pons). This obliterates bilateral descending corticospinal tracts (producing quadriplegia) and corticobulbar tracts (producing anarthria and bilateral lower cranial nerve paralysis). Horizontal conjugate gaze is lost due to destruction of the bilateral abducens nuclei and PPRF. Crucially, the patient is fully conscious and intact cognitively because the reticular activating system and thalamus remain perfused via collateral flow from the posterior communicating arteries to the rostral midbrain. Voluntary vertical eye movements (CN III) and eyelid opening (levator palpebrae superioris) are controlled by the rostral midbrain tectum (interstitial nucleus of Cajal and rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF) which are spared.

options.text: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery bilaterally causing cerebellar tonsillar herniation; sparing of the pontine reticular formation preserves vertical gaze
options.explanation: Tonsillar herniation compresses the medulla causing respiratory arrest and coma, not preserved conscious vertical ocular signaling.

explanation: LOCKED-IN SYNDROME is caused by thrombosis of the basilar artery trunk producing massive bilateral infarction of the BASIS PONTIS (ventral pons). This obliterates bilateral descending corticospinal tracts (producing quadriplegia) and corticobulbar tracts (producing anarthria and bilateral lower cranial nerve paralysis). Horizontal conjugate gaze is lost due to destruction of the bilateral abducens nuclei and PPRF. Crucially, the patient is fully conscious and intact cognitively because the reticular activating system and thalamus remain perfused via collateral flow from the posterior communicating arteries to the rostral midbrain. Voluntary vertical eye movements (CN III) and eyelid opening (levator palpebrae superioris) are controlled by the rostral midbrain tectum (interstitial nucleus of Cajal and rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF) which are spared. Quadriplegia + anarthria + intact consciousness (normal EEG) + preserved vertical gaze and blinking = Locked-in syndrome -> basilar artery basis pontis infarction, midbrain spared.

Quadriplegia + anarthria + intact consciousness (normal EEG) + preserved vertical gaze and blinking = Locked-in syndrome -> basilar artery basis pontis infarction, midbrain spared.

subject: Anatomy
topic: Weber Syndrome Ventral Midbrain Localization
stem: A 68-year-old man presents with acute onset of double vision and right-sided hemiplegia. Physical examination reveals: the left eye is deviated 'down and out' at rest with severe ptosis; the left pupil is 6 mm and non-reactive to direct light or accommodation (right pupil is 3 mm and reactive); and there is a spastic hemiparesis of the right upper and lower extremities with hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response. Facial sensation and cerebellar coordination are intact. Which of the following arterial branches is occluded in this patient, and what two structures within the brainstem are infarcted?

options.text: Anterior choroidal artery; infarcted structures are the lateral geniculate nucleus and the optic radiations in the temporal lobe
options.explanation: Anterior choroidal artery infarction causes contralateral hemiplegia, hemianesthesia, and homonymous hemianopsia, without isolated ipsilateral dilated pupil or ptosis.

options.text: Paramedian branches of the basilar artery; infarcted structures are the abducens (CN VI) nucleus and the facial nerve genu in the pons
options.explanation: Millard-Gubler syndrome involves CN VI and VII with contralateral hemiplegia in the ventral pons, not CN III with 'down and out' eye.

options.text: Superior cerebellar artery; infarcted structures are the superior cerebellar peduncle and the red nucleus in the midbrain tegmentum
options.explanation: Benedikt syndrome involves the midbrain tegmentum (red nucleus and cerebellothalamic tracts) producing ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral tremor/ataxia, not pure hemiparesis.

options.text: Anterior spinal artery; infarcted structures are the hypoglossal (CN XII) nucleus and the medullary pyramid
options.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome involves CN XII (tongue deviation) and pyramids in the medulla, not CN III in the midbrain.

options.text: Paramedian perforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA); infarcted structures are the ipsilateral oculomotor (CN III) nerve fascicles and the ipsilateral cerebral peduncle (crus cerebri)
options.explanation: Weber syndrome (superior alternating hemiplegia) is a ventral midbrain syndrome caused by occlusion of paramedian perforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) or basilar bifurcation. The infarction affects two key adjacent structures in the ventral midbrain: (1) OCULOMOTOR NERVE (CN III) fascicles exiting the interpeduncular fossa -> ipsilateral CN III palsy ('down and out' eye, complete ptosis, dilated non-reactive pupil); and (2) CEREBRAL PEDUNCLE (crus cerebri) carrying descending corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts -> contralateral spastic hemiparesis and contralateral lower facial weakness.

Ipsilateral CN III palsy (down and out, dilated pupil, ptosis) + contralateral hemiparesis = Weber syndrome -> ventral midbrain (crus cerebri + CN III) from paramedian PCA branches.

subject: Anatomy
topic: Parinaud Syndrome Dorsal Midbrain Pinealoma
stem: A 14-year-old boy presents with progressive headaches, morning vomiting, and diplopia. Physical examination reveals: complete inability to elevate the eyes voluntarily or on pursuit (upward gaze paralysis), while downward and horizontal saccades are fully preserved; bilateral eyelid retraction with sclera visible above the superior limbus in primary gaze (Collier sign); and pupils that constrict promptly during near accommodation (convergence) but do not constrict to direct light stimulation (light-near dissociation). Bilateral papilledema is present. Neuroimaging demonstrates a 2.5-cm circumscribed mass in the pineal region compressing the dorsal midbrain and causing obstructive non-communicating hydrocephalus of the cerebral aqueduct. Which of the following anatomical structures is directly compressed to produce this patient's vertical gaze palsy?

options.text: The rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (riMLF) and the posterior commissure in the dorsal midbrain pretectal area
options.explanation: Parinaud syndrome (dorsal midbrain syndrome) is caused by compression or infarction of the midbrain tectum and pretectal area, most commonly by a PINEALOMA or hydrocephalus expanding the cerebral aqueduct. The pathognomonic triad includes: (1) UPWARD GAZE PALSY: due to compression of the vertical gaze center located in the rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF (riMLF), interstitial nucleus of Cajal, and the POSTERIOR COMMISSURE (fibers mediating upward gaze cross in the posterior commissure); (2) LIGHT-NEAR DISSOCIATION (pseudo-Argyll Robertson pupils): compression of the pretectal nuclei abolishes the light reflex afferents to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei while sparing the ventral cortical pathway for the near response; and (3) CONVERGENCE-RETRACTION NYSTAGMUS and COLLIER SIGN (eyelid retraction due to posterior commissure disinhibition).

options.text: The abducens nucleus and the paramedian pontine reticular formation in the caudal dorsal pons
options.explanation: PPRF and CN VI nucleus mediate horizontal conjugate gaze in the pons, not vertical upward gaze in the dorsal midbrain.

options.text: The Edinger-Westphal parasympathetic nucleus and the medial longitudinal fasciculus in the ventral midbrain
options.explanation: Edinger-Westphal mediates pupilloconstriction; pure destruction causes fixed dilated pupils, not selective upward gaze palsy with light-near dissociation.

options.text: The lateral geniculate nucleus and the Meyer loop in the temporal lobe
options.explanation: Lateral geniculate nucleus and Meyer loop mediate visual field perception (pie-in-the-sky quadrantanopia), not motor ocular motility.

options.text: The frontal eye fields in the caudal middle frontal gyrus
options.explanation: Frontal eye fields generate contralateral horizontal saccades; vertical gaze is organized in the midbrain tectum.

explanation: Parinaud syndrome (dorsal midbrain syndrome) is caused by compression or infarction of the midbrain tectum and pretectal area, most commonly by a PINEALOMA or hydrocephalus expanding the cerebral aqueduct. The pathognomonic triad includes: (1) UPWARD GAZE PALSY: due to compression of the vertical gaze center located in the rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF (riMLF), interstitial nucleus of Cajal, and the POSTERIOR COMMISSURE (fibers mediating upward gaze cross in the posterior commissure); (2) LIGHT-NEAR DISSOCIATION (pseudo-Argyll Robertson pupils): compression of the pretectal nuclei abolishes the light reflex afferents to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei while sparing the ventral cortical pathway for the near response; and (3) CONVERGENCE-RETRACTION NYSTAGMUS and COLLIER SIGN (eyelid retraction due to posterior commissure disinhibition). Pineal mass + upward gaze palsy + light-near dissociation + bilateral eyelid retraction (Collier sign) = Parinaud syndrome -> pretectal area / posterior commissure compression.

subject: Anatomy
topic: Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia MLF Demyelination
stem: A 28-year-old woman with a history of optic neuritis presents with horizontal double vision. On physical examination, when the patient attempts to look to the right, conjugate gaze is normal. However, when instructed to look to the left, the left eye abducts fully and exhibits prominent horizontal, coarse, rhythmic nystagmus, while the right eye fails to adduct past the midline. When the patient is subsequently asked to look at a pen brought toward the bridge of her nose (convergence testing), both the right and left eyes adduct completely and symmetrically. Which of the following anatomical structures is affected by demyelination in this patient?

options.text: The left abducens (CN VI) nucleus in the caudal dorsolateral pons
options.explanation: A left abducens nucleus lesion causes complete left horizontal gaze palsy: neither the left eye can abduct nor the right eye adduct on attempted left gaze.

options.text: The right medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) in the dorsal brainstem tegmentum
options.explanation: This patient has an INTERNUCLEAR OPHTHALMOPLEGIA (INO), classic for multiple sclerosis in young adults. Horizontal conjugate gaze is coordinated by the abducens nucleus (CN VI) in the pons: abducens interneurons cross the midline and ascend via the MEDIAL LONGITUDINAL FASCICULUS (MLF) to synapse on the contralateral oculomotor nucleus (CN III) in the midbrain, driving the contralateral medial rectus to adduct. A lesion in the RIGHT MLF prevents the signal from reaching the right medial rectus when looking to the left (impaired adduction of the right eye). The left abducting eye exhibits compensatory nystagmus. Crucially, CONVERGENCE IS PRESERVED because convergence signals originate in the cortex and travel directly to the Edinger-Westphal and oculomotor nuclei via the pretectal area, completely bypassing the MLF.

options.text: The right oculomotor (CN III) nerve fascicle in the interpeduncular fossa
options.explanation: An oculomotor nerve lesion would paralyze the right medial rectus during BOTH conjugate gaze AND convergence, whereas convergence is fully intact here.

options.text: The left paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF)
options.explanation: A PPRF lesion causes inability to initiate all saccades toward the ipsilateral (left) side, not an isolated adduction deficit with contralateral nystagmus.

options.text: The optic chiasm in the anterior cranial fossa
options.explanation: Optic chiasm lesions cause bitemporal hemianopsia without affecting ocular motor cranial nerves or conjugate gaze.

explanation: This patient has an INTERNUCLEAR OPHTHALMOPLEGIA (INO), classic for multiple sclerosis in young adults. Horizontal conjugate gaze is coordinated by the abducens nucleus (CN VI) in the pons: abducens interneurons cross the midline and ascend via the MEDIAL LONGITUDINAL FASCICULUS (MLF) to synapse on the contralateral oculomotor nucleus (CN III) in the midbrain, driving the contralateral medial rectus to adduct. A lesion in the RIGHT MLF prevents the signal from reaching the right medial rectus when looking to the left (impaired adduction of the right eye). The left abducting eye exhibits compensatory nystagmus. Crucially, CONVERGENCE IS PRESERVED because convergence signals originate in the cortex and travel directly to the Edinger-Westphal and oculomotor nuclei via the pretectal area, completely bypassing the MLF. Attempted left gaze -> right eye cannot adduct, left eye abducts with nystagmus; convergence INTACT = Right Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO) -> Right MLF lesion.

subject: Anatomy
topic: Horner Syndrome First vs Second vs Third Order Localization
stem: A 56-year-old male heavy smoker presents with right shoulder pain, numbness radiating down the medial aspect of his right forearm to the fourth and fifth fingers, and hoarseness. Physical examination reveals mild right upper eyelid ptosis and pupillary miosis (right pupil 2.5 mm, left pupil 5 mm in dim light); pupillary dilation in dim light is markedly delayed on the right. Anhydrosis is noted over the right forehead, cheek, and neck, but sweating is normal over the right arm and trunk. Chest radiograph demonstrates an apical mass in the superior pulmonary sulcus of the right lung (Pancoast tumor). Demyelination or compression of which of the following neural structures is responsible for the pupillary and eyelid abnormalities in this patient?

options.text: First-order central sympathetic neurons descending from the posterior hypothalamus through the lateral medullary reticular formation
options.explanation: First-order lesions occur in brainstem strokes (Wallenberg syndrome) and cervical spinal cord trauma (syringomyelia), not apical pulmonary tumors.

options.text: Third-order postganglionic sympathetic fibers ascending within the adventitia of the internal carotid artery
options.explanation: Third-order lesions occur with internal carotid artery dissection or cavernous sinus lesions, causing ptosis and miosis WITHOUT facial anhidrosis (sudomotor fibers travel with external carotid).

options.text: Second-order preganglionic sympathetic fibers exiting the ciliospinal center of Budge (C8-T2) through the white rami communicantes traversing the thoracic apex to the superior cervical ganglion

subject: Anatomy
topic: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis Abducens Nerve Vulnerability
stem: A 26-year-old woman develops a painful furuncle in the nasolabial fold (the 'danger triangle' of the face) that she vigorously squeezed. Three days later, she presents to the emergency department with high fever, severe periorbital edema, chemosis, proptosis, and severe retro-orbital headache. Neurological examination reveals that when the patient is instructed to look laterally to the right, the right eye fails completely to abduct past the midline. When she attempts to look in other directions, partial weakness of right eye elevation, depression, and adduction is noted, along with numbness over the right forehead and cheek. Corneal reflex is diminished on the right. Contrast-enhanced MRI reveals thrombosis of the right cavernous sinus. Which of the following cranial nerves was impaired first and most severely because of its unique anatomical position floating freely within the interior of the cavernous sinus adjacent to the internal carotid artery?

options.text: Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
options.explanation: CN III courses along the superior aspect of the lateral dural wall of the sinus and is involved later as thrombosis expands.

options.text: Trochlear nerve (CN IV)
options.explanation: CN IV is situated within the lateral fibrous wall below CN III and is protected from initial intracavernous pressure.

options.text: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1)
options.explanation: CN V1 travels in the lateral wall beneath CN IV, mediating corneal sensation.

options.text: Abducens nerve (CN VI)
options.explanation: The cavernous sinus is a dural venous sinus situated on either side of the sella turcica. Venous drainage from the facial 'danger triangle' flows via the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins into the cavernous sinus. The ABDUCENS NERVE (CN VI) has a unique anatomical trajectory: unlike all other cranial nerves in the sinus, CN VI does NOT travel within the protective fibrous lateral dural wall; instead, it FLOATS FREELY WITHIN THE CENTER of the cavernous sinus cavity, immediately adjacent to the cavernous segment of the internal carotid artery. Consequently, elevated intracavernous pressure, thrombosis, or aneurysm of the ICA compresses CN VI earliest and most severely, causing isolated abducens palsy (lateral rectus failure) prior to the involvement of CN III, IV, V1, and V2 located safely in the lateral wall.

options.text: Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V2)
options.explanation: CN V2 travels along the inferolateral wall before exiting via the foramen rotundum; it is not free-floating in the cavernous lumen.

subject: Anatomy
topic: Visual Pathway Lesions Meyer vs Baum Loop Quadrantanopia
stem: A 32-year-old man undergoes surgical resection of a low-grade oligodendroglioma in the right temporal lobe. On postoperative neuro-ophthalmologic assessment, automated Humphrey visual field perimetry is performed. The patient is found to have a complete, dense visual field defect restricted entirely to the left superior quadrant in both eyes (contralateral superior homonymous quadrantanopia / 'pie-in-the-sky' defect). Visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes, and pupillary light reflexes are normal and symmetrical. Which of the following components of the visual pathway was severed during the surgical approach through the temporal lobe?

options.text: Baum loop of the optic radiations passing directly posterior through the parietal lobe stria medullaris
options.explanation: Baum loop courses through the parietal lobe and carries fibers from the superior retina (inferior visual field); lesions produce a 'pie-on-the-floor' inferior quadrantanopia.

options.text: Nasal fibers of the left optic nerve decussating in the anterior optic chiasm (Wilbrand knee)
options.explanation: Decussating nasal fibers at the chiasm cause bitemporal hemianopsia, not a homonymous quadrantanopia.

options.text: The main optic tract looping around the ipsilateral cerebral peduncle
options.explanation: Optic tract lesions cause a complete contralateral homonymous hemianopsia (all 4 quadrants), not a selective quadrantanopia.

options.text: The superior colliculus and pretectal nuclei in the rostral midbrain tegmentum
options.explanation: Superior colliculus and pretectal lesions affect the pupillary light reflex and vertical gaze (Parinaud syndrome), not conscious visual fields.

options.text: Meyer loop of the optic radiations looping anteriorly and inferiorly through the temporal lobe around the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle
options.explanation: Optic radiations project from the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) to the primary visual cortex (calcarine sulcus). The fibers split into two distinct bundles: (1) MEYER LOOP (inferior optic radiations): fibers representing the SUPERIOR visual field loop anteriorly and inferiorly through the TEMPORAL LOBE around the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle before terminating on the inferior bank of the calcarine sulcus (lingual gyrus). Lesions in the temporal lobe disrupt Meyer loop, producing a CONTRALATERAL SUPERIOR HOMONYMOUS QUADRANTANOPIA ('pie in the sky'); (2) BAUM LOOP (superior optic radiations): fibers representing the INFERIOR visual field course directly through the PARIETAL LOBE to the superior bank of the calcarine sulcus (cuneus); lesions cause contralateral INFERIOR quadrantanopia ('pie on the floor').

explanation: Optic radiations project from the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) to the primary visual cortex (calcarine sulcus). Temporal lobe lesion + contralateral upper visual field defect ('pie in the sky') = Meyer loop severance (inferior optic radiations).

subject: Anatomy
topic: Occipital Cortex Stroke Macular Sparing Dual Perfusion
stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with acute difficulty seeing objects on her right side. Visual field testing demonstrates a dense right homonymous hemianopsia; however, formal perimetric mapping reveals complete preservation of central visual acuity (20/20 bilaterally) and an intact central visual field measuring 5 degrees around the fovea in both eyes ('macular sparing'). Pupillary light reflexes are brisk and equal bilaterally. Brain MRI demonstrates an acute ischemic infarction of the medial surface of the left occipital lobe along the calcarine sulcus. Which of the following vascular anatomical features explains the preservation of central macular vision in this patient?

options.text: The left posterior cerebral artery (PCA) was occluded, but the caudal occipital pole cortex representing the fovea is supplied by collateral blood flow from the middle cerebral artery (MCA)
options.explanation: The primary visual cortex (striate cortex / Brodmann area 17) is located on the banks of the calcarine sulcus in the occipital lobe and is supplied primarily by the POSTERIOR CEREBRAL ARTERY (PCA). Occlusion of the PCA causes contralateral homonymous hemianopsia. However, the occipital pole (caudal visual cortex), which has a massive overrepresentation dedicated entirely to the central macula/fovea, possesses a DUAL BLOOD SUPPLY: it receives collateral branches from the terminal arborizations of the MIDDLE CEREBRAL ARTERY (MCA) as well as the PCA. In isolated PCA occlusion, the MCA collateral flow maintains perfusion to the occipital pole, preserving central visual acuity and central visual field ('MACULAR SPARING').

options.text: Macular fibers cross twice within the optic chiasm, projecting bilaterally to both lateral geniculate nuclei
options.explanation: Macular fibers do not project bilaterally; hemiretinal representation follows the same unilateral crossing rules as peripheral fibers.

options.text: Central foveal ganglion cell axons bypass the primary visual cortex entirely to synapse directly in the frontal eye fields
options.explanation: Conscious visual perception requires striate cortex; foveal axons do not bypass the visual cortex to go to frontal eye fields.

options.text: The anterior choroidal artery provides retrograde perfusion to the entire length of the calcarine sulcus
options.explanation: The anterior choroidal artery supplies the optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, and posterior limb of the internal capsule, not the calcarine cortex.

options.text: Anterior communicating artery collaterals maintain continuous pressure in the posterior communicating artery
options.explanation: ACOM collaterals supply the ACA distribution; macular sparing is mediated by MCA-PCA terminal watershed collaterals at the occipital pole.

explanation: The primary visual cortex (striate cortex / Brodmann area 17) is located on the banks of the calcarine sulcus in the occipital lobe and is supplied primarily by the POSTERIOR CEREBRAL ARTERY (PCA). Occlusion of the PCA causes contralateral homonymous hemianopsia. Left PCA stroke + right homonymous hemianopsia with central visual acuity intact = Macular sparing -> dual blood supply to occipital pole from MCA collaterals.

subject: Pathology
topic: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus Triad and Tap Test
stem: A 74-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his daughter because of progressive walking difficulty, urinary accidents, and memory problems over the past 8 months. Physical examination reveals a slow, wide-based, shuffling gait; his feet appear glued to the floor when initiating steps ('magnetic gait'). He has mild short-term memory impairment (MoCA score 21/30) and urgency urinary incontinence. Muscle strength and sensation are normal. Brain MRI demonstrates symmetrical, massive enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles out of proportion to cerebral cortical sulcal widening, with a rounded frontal horn contour and thinning of the corpus callosum. A high-volume diagnostic lumbar puncture (removal of 40 mL of CSF) demonstrates a normal opening pressure of 140 mm H2O (normal 70-200 mm H2O); immediately following the procedure, the patient demonstrates marked, objective improvement in gait velocity and stride length. Which of the following is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism of this condition?

options.text: Direct obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius by an ependymal web causing non-communicating hydrocephalus
options.explanation: Aqueductal stenosis causes non-communicating hydrocephalus with elevated opening pressure and severe headaches, not NPH.

options.text: Impaired cerebrospinal fluid resorption at the arachnoid granulations leading to intermittent episodic pressure waves that stretch paracentral motor fibers of the corona radiata and corticospinal tracts innervating the legs
options.explanation: Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) is a form of communicating hydrocephalus presenting with the classic triad of 'WET, WACKY, and WOBBLY': Gait disturbance (magnetic, apraxic gait; earliest and most responsive to shunt), Dementia (subcortical executive dysfunction), and Urinary incontinence (detrusor instability). The primary pathology is decreased CSF absorption across the ARACHNOID GRANULATIONS into the dural venous sinuses (due to prior subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis, or idiopathic fibrosis). CSF accumulates, expanding the lateral ventricles and exerting mechanical traction on the SACRAL AND PARACENTRAL MOTOR FIBERS of the corona radiata which loop closely around the ventricles to innervate the lower extremities and bladder. Removal of CSF (tap test) temporarily relieves this distortion, confirming candidacy for ventriculoperitoneal shunting.

options.text: Selective autoimmune destruction of cholinergic projection neurons in the basal nucleus of Meynert
options.explanation: Loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert occurs in Alzheimer disease, which features memory loss without early magnetic gait or urinary incontinence.

options.text: Intracellular accumulation of alpha-synuclein aggregates within the substantia nigra pars compacta
options.explanation: Substantia nigra synuclein loss defines Parkinson disease (resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity), which does not present with massive ventricular dilation or normal-pressure tap test response.

options.text: Autoimmune demyelination of the central pontine myelin sheaths within the basis pontis
options.explanation: Central pontine myelinolysis causes spastic quadriparesis and pseudobulbar palsy following rapid hyponatremia correction, not chronic NPH.

Magnetic gait + memory loss + urinary incontinence + ventricular enlargement with normal opening pressure + improvement after tap = NPH -> impaired arachnoid resorption.

subject: Pharmacology
topic: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Acetazolamide Target
stem: A 24-year-old obese woman (BMI 36 kg/m2) presents with daily throbbing headaches that are worse upon awakening and exacerbated by coughing. She describes hearing a rhythmic 'whooshing' sound in both ears that matches her heartbeat (pulsatile tinnitus), along with brief episodes of darkened vision when bending over. Physical examination reveals bilateral papilledema and failure of the left eye to fully abduct on lateral gaze (left CN VI palsy). Visual field testing shows enlarged blind spots bilaterally. Brain MRI is normal, demonstrating an empty sella and flattening of the posterior globes, with no mass or hydrocephalus. Magnetic resonance venography confirms patent dural sinuses. Lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position demonstrates an opening pressure of 320 mm H2O (markedly elevated) with normal CSF constituents. Which of the following medications is the first-line pharmacotherapy for this condition, and what is its specific molecular target in the choroid plexus?

options.text: Furosemide; inhibits apical NKCC2 cotransporters in the ependymal lining of the third ventricle
options.explanation: NKCC2 is expressed in the renal thick ascending limb, not choroid plexus; furosemide is a secondary adjunct, but acetazolamide is first-line.

options.text: Topiramate; selectively blocks voltage-gated T-type calcium channels in the subarachnoid trabeculae
options.explanation: Topiramate has mild carbonic anhydrase activity and promotes weight loss, but does not act on T-type calcium channels in subarachnoid trabeculae.

options.text: Acetazolamide; inhibits carbonic anhydrase in choroid plexus epithelial cells to decrease bicarbonate-dependent cerebrospinal fluid secretion
options.explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) is most common in young, overweight women, and is linked to vitamin A toxicity, tetracyclines, and obesity. Elevated ICP produces headache, pulsatile tinnitus, papilledema, transient visual obscurations, and false localizing CN VI palsy (stretched over the petrous ridge). Opening pressure is >250 mm H2O with normal CSF. The first-line medical therapy to prevent permanent visual loss is ACETAZOLAMIDE. Acetazolamide inhibits CARBONIC ANHYDRASE in the choroid plexus epithelium, reducing HCO3- generation and basolateral/apical transport, which decreases total CSF production by up to 50%.

options.text: Mannitol; directly opens aquaporin-1 channels on ventricular ependymal cells to promote CSF drainage
options.explanation: Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic used intravenously for acute cerebral herniation emergencies, not chronic ambulatory maintenance.

options.text: Spironolactone; competitively blocks mineralocorticoid receptors on the arachnoid villi
options.explanation: Mineralocorticoid receptors on arachnoid villi are not the target; the therapeutic mechanism is carbonic anhydrase inhibition in the choroid plexus.

subject: Pathology
topic: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Xanthochromia and Berry Aneurysms
stem: A 46-year-old woman presents to the emergency department clutching her head, stating she has just experienced 'the worst headache of my life' (thunderclap headache) that reached peak maximal intensity within 30 seconds while lifting a heavy box. She has severe photophobia and vomiting. Physical examination shows blood pressure 168/98 mm Hg, nuchal rigidity, and a positive Kernig sign; there are no focal motor deficits. Non-contrast head CT performed 16 hours after symptom onset is completely normal. A lumbar puncture is subsequently performed. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis reveals an opening pressure of 240 mm H2O, 12,000 RBCs/microL in tube 1 and 11,800 RBCs/microL in tube 4, and persistent yellow pigmentation of the supernatant after centrifugation (xanthochromia) confirmed by spectrophotometry. Which of the following is the most likely location of the vascular lesion responsible for this condition, and what biochemical process produces the yellow CSF supernatant?

options.text: Rupture of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms in the lenticulostriate arteries; xanthochromia results from rapid oxidation of myoglobin into metmyoglobin
options.explanation: Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms cause intraparenchymal basal ganglia hemorrhage, not primary subarachnoid hemorrhage with xanthochromia.

options.text: Tearing of cortical bridging veins draining into the superior sagittal sinus; xanthochromia results from acute hemosiderin clearance
options.explanation: Tearing of bridging veins causes subdural hematomas (crescentic on CT), not aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage with thunderclap headache.

options.text: Laceration of the middle meningeal artery underneath the pterion; xanthochromia results from rapid biliverdin crystallization
options.explanation: Middle meningeal artery rupture causes epidural hematoma with a lucid interval and lens-shaped biconvex mass, not diffuse SAH with xanthochromia.

options.text: Rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm at the junction of the anterior communicating artery and anterior cerebral artery; xanthochromia results from macrophage catabolism of extravasated oxyhemoglobin into bilirubin
options.explanation: Non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is most commonly caused by rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm, located in 85% of cases in the anterior circulation (most commonly the ANTERIOR COMMUNICATING ARTERY [ACOM], followed by PCOM and MCA bifurcation). Thunderclap headache reaching peak intensity in <1 minute with meningismus is classic. If non-contrast CT is negative (sensitivity decreases after 6-12 hours), LUMBAR PUNCTURE is mandatory. True SAH is distinguished from a traumatic tap by: (1) Equal RBC counts across all 4 collection tubes; and (2) XANTHOCHROMIA (yellow CSF supernatant). Xanthochromia takes 4-12 hours to develop as subarachnoid macrophages catabolize lysed RBC oxyhemoglobin into BILIRUBIN (which persists for 2-4 weeks).

options.text: Dissection of the petrous segment of the internal carotid artery; xanthochromia results from high concentrations of albumin
options.explanation: Carotid dissection causes Horner syndrome and stroke, not diffuse aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage with thunderclap headache.

subject: Anatomy
topic: Epidural Hematoma Middle Meningeal Artery Pterion
stem: A 20-year-old collegiate hockey player is struck violently on the left temple by a puck. He experiences a brief loss of consciousness lasting 1 minute, after which he awakens completely alert, oriented, and symptom-free ('lucid interval'). Two hours later, he complains of an excruciating headache and rapidly becomes somnolent and unresponsive. On arrival at the trauma center, his blood pressure is 180/100 mm Hg, pulse is 48/min, and respirations are 10/min (Cushing triad). The left pupil is dilated to 7 mm and fixed to light, with right-sided hemiplegia. Emergent non-contrast head CT demonstrates a hyperdense, biconvex, lenticular-shaped extra-axial mass underneath the left pterion that does NOT cross cranial suture lines. Laceration of which of the following vessels is responsible for this hematoma, and what foramen does this vessel traverse to enter the cranium?

options.text: Bridging cortical veins draining into the superior sagittal sinus; enters the cranium through the jugular foramen
options.explanation: Bridging veins tear in subdural hematomas, which form crescentic collections crossing suture lines in elderly patients.

options.text: Superficial temporal artery; enters the cranium through the foramen rotundum
options.explanation: The superficial temporal artery is an external scalp vessel and foramen rotundum transmits CN V2, not middle meningeal vessels.

options.text: Posterior communicating artery; enters the cranium through the carotid canal
options.explanation: PCOM is an intradural circle of Willis artery whose aneurysm compresses CN III, not an extradural vessel fractured by pterion trauma.

options.text: Internal carotid artery; enters the cranium through the foramen lacerum
options.explanation: The ICA enters via the carotid canal, traverses the cavernous sinus, and its rupture produces carotid-cavernous fistulas, not epidural hematomas.

options.text: Middle meningeal artery (a branch of the maxillary artery); enters the cranium through the foramen spinosum
options.explanation: Epidural hematoma is caused by blunt trauma to the PTERION (the thin junction of frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones on the lateral skull). Deep to the pterion lies the anterior branch of the MIDDLE MENINGEAL ARTERY, which arises from the maxillary artery (a terminal branch of the external carotid) and enters the cranial cavity through the FORAMEN SPINOSUM. subject: Pathology
topic: Subdural Hematoma Bridging Vein Tearing Mechanism
stem: An 82-year-old man with mild Alzheimer disease and chronic alcohol use is evaluated for progressive confusion, lethargy, and unsteady gait over the past 3 weeks. His daughter recalls that he bumped his head against a kitchen cabinet a month ago, but appeared fine at the time. Physical examination reveals mild left pronator drift, hyperreflexia on the left, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Non-contrast head CT demonstrates a crescent-shaped, concave, hypodense extra-axial fluid collection overlying the entire right cerebral hemisphere that crosses the coronal and lambdoid suture lines, but is limited by the falx cerebri, with a 6-mm midline shift. Tearing of which of the following vascular structures is responsible for this patient's subacute neurological deterioration?

options.text: Bridging cortical veins traversing the subdural space to drain into the superior sagittal sinus, rendered vulnerable by cerebral cortical atrophy
options.explanation: Subdural hematoma (SDH) is caused by rupture of BRIDGING CORTICAL VEINS as they traverse the potential space between the arachnoid mater and the inner dural border cell layer to drain into the superior sagittal sinus. In elderly patients and chronic alcoholics, progressive BRAIN ATROPHY increases the distance between the brain surface and the dural sinuses, placing bridging veins under chronic mechanical tension. Even minor head trauma shears these fragile low-pressure veins. Venous bleeding accumulates slowly over days to weeks (chronic/subacute SDH), forming a CRESCENT-SHAPED concave collection that CROSSES CRANIAL SUTURE LINES (because blood is in the subdural space, not attached to sutures), but is restricted by the rigid dural reflections (falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli).

options.text: Middle meningeal artery stripping the periosteal dura from the inner table of the calvarium
options.explanation: Middle meningeal artery rupture causes epidural hematoma with a biconvex shape restricted by cranial sutures, not a crescent crossing sutures.

options.text: Anterior cerebral artery branches penetrating the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
options.explanation: ACA penetrating branches supply medial cerebral parenchyma; rupture causes intraparenchymal hemorrhage, not subdural hematomas.

options.text: Basilar vein of Rosenthal entering the straight sinus within the tentorium cerebelli
options.explanation: The vein of Rosenthal is a deep cerebral vein whose thrombosis causes deep venous infarction, not chronic hemispheric subdural hematoma.

options.text: Sphenoparietal dural venous sinus beneath the lesser wing of the sphenoid
options.explanation: The sphenoparietal sinus drains into the cavernous sinus; bridging veins over the cerebral convexities are the classic source of hemispheric subdural hematoma.

subject: Pathology
topic: Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome Presynaptic VGCC
stem: A 64-year-old man who is a 40 pack-year cigarette smoker presents with progressive proximal muscle weakness, stating that he has difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs. Interestingly, he notes that his muscle strength noticeably improves after brief physical activity ('warm-up phenomenon'). He also reports dry mouth and erectile dysfunction. Physical examination reveals bilateral proximal leg weakness (3/5 strength in hip flexors) that increases to 4+/5 after 15 seconds of maximum voluntary contraction; deep tendon reflexes are 0/4 at the knees and ankles at baseline, but become briskly 2+/4 immediately after exercise. Chest CT demonstrates a 4-cm central hilar mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Repetitive nerve stimulation at high frequency (50 Hz) demonstrates an incremental compound muscle action potential (CMAP) response (>200% increase). Which of the following is the target of the autoantibodies in this patient?

options.text: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChR) on the postsynaptic junctional folds
options.explanation: Postsynaptic AChR antibodies cause Myasthenia Gravis, which features ocular/bulbar weakness that WORSENS with exercise, normal reflexes, no autonomic symptoms, and a DECREMENTAL response on nerve stimulation.

options.text: P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC) on the presynaptic motor nerve terminal
options.explanation: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is a paraneoplastic autoimmune disorder occurring in ~3% of patients with SMALL CELL LUNG CANCER (SCLC), which expresses neuroendocrine voltage-gated calcium channels. Autoantibodies target PRESYNAPTIC P/Q-TYPE VOLTAGE-GATED CALCIUM CHANNELS (VGCC) at the neuromuscular junction. Blockade of Ca2+ influx prevents SNARE-mediated acetylcholine vesicle exocytosis. options.text: Muscle-specific receptor tyrosine kinase (MuSK) on the postsynaptic membrane
options.explanation: MuSK antibodies occur in generalized myasthenia gravis, causing postsynaptic receptor dispersion and decremental response without autonomic dysfunction.

options.text: Presynaptic synaptobrevin and syntaxin SNARE complex proteins
options.explanation: SNARE proteins are cleaved by botulinum and tetanus neurotoxins, not targeted by paraneoplastic autoantibodies in small cell lung cancer.

options.text: Voltage-gated potassium channels (VGKC) in the peripheral nerve myelin sheath
options.explanation: VGKC antibodies cause Isaacs syndrome (neuromyotonia with continuous muscle fiber activity) and Morvan syndrome, not LEMS with incremental CMAP.

subject: Pathology
topic: Myasthenia Gravis Postsynaptic AChR and Decremental Response
stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with fluctuating double vision and drooping of both eyelids that becomes progressively worse toward the evening. Over the past month, she has also noticed difficulty chewing tough food toward the end of a meal and weakness in her arms when blow-drying her hair. Physical examination shows bilateral asymmetric ptosis that worsens after 60 seconds of sustained upward gaze (curtain sign). Deep tendon reflexes are normal (2+/4) and symmetrical, and sensation is intact. Applying an ice pack over her closed eyelids for 2 minutes produces significant resolution of the ptosis. Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrates an anterior mediastinal mass consistent with a thymoma. Repetitive nerve stimulation at low frequency (3 Hz) demonstrates a >15% progressive decrease in the compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitude (decremental response). Which of the following is the underlying molecular mechanism of this disorder?

options.text: Autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels preventing acetylcholine vesicle exocytosis
options.explanation: Presynaptic VGCC antibodies cause Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, where strength improves with activity and deep tendon reflexes are absent.

options.text: Autoimmune-mediated destruction of myelin basic protein in peripheral motor nerve axons
options.explanation: Myelin destruction causes Guillain-Barré syndrome (AIDP), presenting with ascending flaccid paralysis and absent reflexes, not fluctuating ocular ptosis with thymoma.

options.text: Antibody- and complement-mediated destruction of postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, accompanied by flattening and simplification of the synaptic junctional folds
options.explanation: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder caused by autoantibodies directed against POSTSYNAPTIC NICOTINIC ACETYLCHOLINE RECEPTORS (AChR) on the motor endplate. Pathogenic mechanisms include: (1) Complement-mediated lysis of junctional folds via the membrane attack complex (C5b-9), leading to morphological flattening and loss of receptor density; (2) Accelerated endocytosis and degradation of cross-linked AChRs; and (3) Functional receptor blockade. The classic presentation is fluctuating, fatigable weakness of ocular (ptosis, diplopia) and bulbar muscles, worsening with activity/evening. Deep tendon reflexes are NORMAL. The ice pack test improves ptosis because lower temperatures inhibit acetylcholinesterase activity. Repetitive nerve stimulation shows a DECREMENTAL CMAP response. 75% have thymic follicular hyperplasia and 15% have thymoma.

options.text: Antibodies targeting ryanodine receptors (RYR1) causing uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
options.explanation: RYR1 mutations cause malignant hyperthermia, not fatigable ocular weakness with thymoma.

options.text: Proteolytic cleavage of synaptosomal synaptotagmin preventing vesicular fusion
options.explanation: Botulinum neurotoxin cleaves SNARE proteins causing descending paralysis; MG is mediated by anti-postsynaptic AChR autoantibodies.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Botulinum Neurotoxin SNARE Proteolysis Mechanism
stem: A 38-year-old man presents with blurred vision, dry mouth, and difficulty swallowing 24 hours after consuming home-canned asparagus. Physical examination reveals bilateral symmetric ptosis, fixed dilated pupils (pupillary light reflex absent), dysarthria, and dysphagia. Over the next 12 hours, he develops progressive, symmetric, descending flaccid weakness affecting his neck, arms, and respiratory muscles. Sensory examination is completely normal, and deep tendon reflexes are absent in all extremities. Which of the following is the precise molecular mechanism of the bacterial toxin causing this clinical syndrome?

options.text: Retrograde intra-axonal transport to spinal cord Renshaw cells where it cleaves synaptobrevin to block GABA and glycine release
options.explanation: Retrograde axonal transport to spinal Renshaw inhibitory cells describes tetanospasmin (Clostridium tetani), causing disinhibition and SPASTIC paralysis (trismus, risus sardonicus).

options.text: ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2 (EF-2) halting protein synthesis in peripheral nerve axons
options.explanation: ADP-ribosylation of EF-2 is the mechanism of diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A, causing pseudomembranous pharyngitis and myocarditis.

options.text: Pore formation in erythrocyte and motor neuron membranes mediated by cholesterol-dependent cytolysins
options.explanation: Cholesterol-dependent cytolysins (e.g. perfringolysin O, streptolysin O) cause membrane lysis, not selective flaccid paralysis via SNARE cleavage.

options.text: Zinc-dependent endopeptidase cleavage of SNARE proteins (synaptobrevin, SNAP-25, and syntaxin) preventing acetylcholine exocytosis at peripheral cholinergic synapses
options.explanation: Clostridium botulinum produces botulinum neurotoxin, an AB subunit zinc-dependent metalloproteinase. The toxin is absorbed from improperly canned food and travels hematogenously to PERIPHERAL CHOLINERGIC SYNAPSES (both neuromuscular junctions and parasympathetic/sympathetic autonomic ganglia). The heavy chain mediates receptor-mediated endocytosis, while the light chain cleaves SNARE PROTEINS (synaptobrevin / VAMP, SNAP-25, and syntaxin). SNARE cleavage prevents the fusion of acetylcholine storage vesicles with the presynaptic plasma membrane, completely blocking acetylcholine exocytosis. This causes DESCENDING FLACCID PARALYSIS with prominent early autonomic/cranial nerve deficits: symmetric bilateral cranial neuropathies (ptosis, fixed dilated pupils, blurred vision), dry mouth, and absent reflexes without sensory loss.

options.text: Stimulation of presynaptic calcium-sensing receptors causing massive neurotransmitter depletion and secondary exhaustion
options.explanation: Black widow spider venom (alpha-latrotoxin) stimulates massive transmitter release; botulinum toxin inhibits release via SNARE cleavage.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Tetanus Toxin Retrograde Transport and Renshaw Disinhibition
stem: A 42-year-old unimmunized farm laborer presents with painful jaw stiffness, difficulty chewing, and a stiff neck 8 days after stepping on a rusty nail in a barnyard. Physical examination reveals a spastic grimace with sustained contraction of the facial muscles (risus sardonicus) and severe involuntary spasm of the masseter muscles preventing mouth opening (trismus / lockjaw). While being examined in a brightly lit room, a sudden loud sound triggers generalized, violent, painful muscle spasms with severe hyperextension of the spine and neck (opisthotonos). Mentation is completely alert and intact. Which of the following describes the route of neurotoxin spread and its cellular site of action?

options.text: Hematogenous dissemination to peripheral autonomic ganglia where it permanently binds and hyperactivates postsynaptic muscarinic M3 receptors
options.explanation: Tetanus toxin does not hyperactivate muscarinic receptors; it blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter release in the central nervous system.

options.text: Antegrade transport through sensory afferent fibers to the thalamus, causing bilateral thalamocortical desynchronization
options.explanation: Transport is retrograde via motor axons to spinal cord inhibitory interneurons, not antegrade sensory transport to the thalamus.

options.text: Local diffusion within skeletal muscle stroma causing persistent opening of sarcoplasmic ryanodine channels
options.explanation: Local muscle diffusion describes direct myotoxins; tetanospasmin acts within the central nervous system at Renshaw cell synapses.

options.text: Selective destruction of upper motor neurons in the primary motor cortex via microglial activation
options.explanation: Upper motor neuron destruction occurs in ALS; tetanus is an acute toxin-mediated disinhibition of spinal reflex arcs without neuronal death.

options.text: Retrograde intra-axonal transport via motor nerves to the spinal cord, where the toxin cleaves synaptobrevin in inhibitory Renshaw interneurons, preventing the release of GABA and glycine
options.explanation: Tetanus is caused by tetanospasmin, an AB subunit zinc-endopeptidase neurotoxin produced by Clostridium tetani in anaerobic puncture wounds. The toxin binds presynaptic motor nerve terminals and undergoes RETROGRADE INTRA-AXONAL TRANSPORT to the motor neuron cell body in the spinal cord and brainstem. It crosses the synaptic cleft to enter INHIBITORY INTERNEURONS (Renshaw cells). The catalytic light chain cleaves SYNAPTOBREVIN (VAMP), preventing the exocytosis of the inhibitory neurotransmitters GLYCINE and GABA. Loss of inhibitory interneuron control leaves alpha motor neurons constitutively uninhibited, causing reflex spasms, spastic paralysis, trismus, risus sardonicus, and opisthotonos triggered by sensory stimuli.

subject: Pathology
topic: Guillain-Barre Syndrome Albuminocytologic Dissociation
stem: A 28-year-old man presents with progressive symmetric weakness in both legs that began 3 days ago and has now ascended to involve his arms. Two weeks ago, he had an episode of severe bloody diarrhea and crampy abdominal pain that resolved spontaneously. Physical examination demonstrates: bilateral flaccid quadriparesis (muscle strength 2/5 in legs, 3/5 in arms); complete absence of deep tendon reflexes in all four extremities (areflexia); and mild stocking-glove paresthesias. Forced vital capacity is 2.1 L (decreased). Lumbar puncture is performed: CSF opening pressure is 160 mm H2O, WBC count is 2 cells/microL (normal 0-5), glucose is 62 mg/dL, and CSF protein is 185 mg/dL (markedly elevated; normal 15-45 mg/dL). Which of the following is the underlying immunologic mechanism responsible for this patient's neuropathy?

options.text: Molecular mimicry between Campylobacter jejuni lipooligosaccharide and human peripheral nerve gangliosides (such as GM1), triggering endoneurial lymphocytic infiltration and macrophage-mediated demyelination
options.explanation: Guillain-Barré syndrome (Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyradiculoneuropathy, AIDP) is an acute post-infectious polyneuropathy most commonly preceded by CAMPYLOBACTER JEJUNI enteritis. The core mechanism is MOLECULAR MIMICRY: bacterial lipooligosaccharides (LOS) share structural homology with human peripheral nerve GANGLIOSIDES (e.g. GM1, GD1a). Autoreactive antibodies and CD4+ T cells target endoneurial antigens, activating complement and recruiting macrophages that strip and phagocytose the myelin sheath from peripheral spinal roots and nerves. Key findings: ascending symmetric flaccid weakness, AREFLEXIA, and ALBUMINOCYTOLOGIC DISSOCIATION (markedly elevated CSF protein with normal CSF WBC count, due to inflamed spinal roots leaking protein into CSF).

options.text: Autoantibodies directed against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors driving complement-mediated motor endplate destruction
options.explanation: AChR antibodies cause Myasthenia Gravis, which features ocular/bulbar fatigable weakness with normal deep tendon reflexes and normal CSF protein.

options.text: Direct viral neurotropism for anterior horn motor neurons in the lumbar spinal cord causing lytic cell necrosis
options.explanation: Anterior horn motor neuron lysis describes poliovirus and West Nile virus (asymmetric flaccid paralysis with CSF pleocytosis), not demyelinating GBS.

options.text: Vasculitic transmural fibrinoid necrosis of the vasa nervorum driven by circulating hepatitis B immune complexes
options.explanation: Vasa nervorum vasculitis causes mononeuritis multiplex in polyarteritis nodosa, not symmetric ascending polyradiculoneuropathy with albuminocytologic dissociation.

options.text: Accumulation of phytanic acid in peripheral myelin sheaths due to peroxisomal enzyme deficiency
options.explanation: Phytanic acid accumulation causes Refsum disease (ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa, ichthyosis), not acute post-infectious ascending paralysis.

subject: Genetics
topic: Charcot-Marie-Tooth Disease PMP22 Duplication
stem: A 17-year-old boy presents for evaluation of frequent ankle sprains and difficulty running. His father and paternal grandfather have similar gait problems and wear leg braces. Physical examination reveals: bilateral high-arched feet (pes cavus), hammer toes, and severe atrophy of the calf and peroneal muscles producing an 'inverted champagne bottle' appearance of the lower legs. There is bilateral foot drop with a high-stepping (steppage) gait. Sensation to vibration and pinprick is diminished over the feet and ankles bilaterally. Deep tendon reflexes are absent at the ankles. Nerve conduction studies demonstrate marked, uniform slowing of motor nerve conduction velocities (< 30 m/s; normal > 50 m/s) in the peroneal and tibial nerves. Sural nerve biopsy reveals redundant concentric Schwann cell cytoplasmic processes wrapping around axons ('onion-bulb' formations). Which of the following genetic alterations is responsible for this patient's disorder?

options.text: A heterozygous point mutation in the survival motor neuron 1 (SMN1) gene on chromosome 5q
options.explanation: SMN1 homozygous deletions cause spinal muscular atrophy (infantile anterior horn cell degeneration), not CMT1A with onion-bulb formation.

options.text: A 1.4-megabase duplication on chromosome 17p11.2 containing the peripheral myelin protein 22 (PMP22) gene
options.explanation: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A (CMT1A) is the most common inherited peripheral neuropathy (autosomal dominant), caused by a submicroscopic 1.4-Mb DUPLICATION on chromosome 17p11.2 encompassing the PMP22 gene. Overexpression of peripheral myelin protein 22 (PMP22) disrupts myelin compaction and Schwann cell differentiation. Repeated cycles of demyelination and remyelination produce characteristic 'ONION-BULB' Schwann cell hyperplasia encircling axons on histology. Clinical presentation includes insidious onset in adolescence of distal muscle weakness and atrophy (peroneal atrophy, 'inverted champagne bottle' legs), bilateral foot drop (steppage gait), PES CAVUS (high arches), hammer toes, sensory loss, and markedly slowed nerve conduction.

options.text: Trinucleotide CTG repeat expansion in the 3'-untranslated region of the DMPK gene on chromosome 19
options.explanation: DMPK CTG expansion causes myotonic dystrophy type 1 (myotonia, cataracts, cardiac conduction defects, frontal balding), not hereditary motor-sensory neuropathy.

options.text: Homozygous GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the first intron of the FXN gene on chromosome 9
options.explanation: FXN GAA expansion causes Friedreich ataxia (spinocerebellar ataxia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, scoliosis, loss of frataxin), not isolated CMT1A neuropathy.

options.text: A missense mutation in the gap junction protein beta-1 (GJB1) gene on the X chromosome
options.explanation: GJB1 mutations cause X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMTX1), but the classic and most frequent cause (>70% of CMT1) with 'inverted champagne bottle' legs is PMP22 duplication on 17p.

explanation: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A (CMT1A) is the most common inherited peripheral neuropathy (autosomal dominant), caused by a submicroscopic 1.4-Mb DUPLICATION on chromosome 17p11.2 encompassing the PMP22 gene. Overexpression of peripheral myelin protein 22 (PMP22) disrupts myelin compaction and Schwann cell differentiation. Repeated cycles of demyelination and remyelination produce characteristic 'ONION-BULB' Schwann cell hyperplasia encircling axons on histology. Clinical presentation includes insidious onset in adolescence of distal muscle weakness and atrophy (peroneal atrophy, 'inverted champagne bottle' legs), bilateral foot drop (steppage gait), PES CAVUS (high arches), hammer toes, sensory loss, and markedly slowed nerve conduction. Pes cavus + hammer toes + 'inverted champagne bottle' calf atrophy + onion-bulb Schwann cells + slow conduction = Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT1A) -> PMP22 duplication on 17p.

subject: Pathology
topic: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Combined UMN and LMN
stem: A 58-year-old man presents with progressive weakness and muscle wasting that began in his right hand 6 months ago and has now spread to his right arm and both legs. He has also noticed difficulty swallowing liquids and dysarthria. Physical examination reveals: prominent atrophy and visible muscle twitching (fasciculations) in the right thenar eminence, interossei, and tongue; 3/5 muscle strength in the right upper and lower extremities; strikingly hyperactive (3+/4) deep tendon reflexes at both biceps, triceps, and patellar tendons; a positive Hoffman sign on the right; and a right extensor plantar response (positive Babinski sign). Sensation to light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception is completely intact throughout all dermatomes. Sphincter tone and voluntary bladder control are normal. Which of the following is the hallmark neuropathological feature of this disease?

options.text: Selective autoimmune-mediated demyelination restricted entirely to the dorsal columns of the spinal cord and dorsal root ganglia
options.explanation: Dorsal column degeneration describes tabes dorsalis (tertiary syphilis) or B12 deficiency, causing sensory ataxia without combined UMN/LMN motor findings.

options.text: Isolated atrophy of the caudate nucleus and putamen accompanied by intranuclear huntingtin polyglutamine inclusions
options.explanation: Caudate atrophy defines Huntington disease (chorea, dementia, personality changes), not combined upper and lower motor neuron degeneration.

options.text: Degeneration and loss of both upper motor neurons in the primary motor cortex (Betz cells) and lower motor neurons in the brainstem motor nuclei and spinal cord anterior horns, with Bunina bodies and TDP-43-positive cytoplasmic inclusions
options.explanation: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder uniquely characterized by the simultaneous degeneration of BOTH UPPER MOTOR NEURONS (corticospinal tracts and primary motor cortex Betz cells) and LOWER MOTOR NEURONS (anterior horn cells of the spinal cord and motor cranial nerve nuclei CN V, VII, IX, X, XII). Clinical hallmarks: LMN signs (muscle atrophy, weakness, fasciculations) coexisting in the SAME limb/segment as UMN signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, Hoffman sign). Crucially, SENSORY, OCULOMOTOR, and AUTONOMIC/BOWEL-BLADDER FUNCTIONS ARE STRICTLY SPARED. Histopathology demonstrates loss of anterior horn motor neurons with reactive astrocytosis, BUNINA BODIES (cystatin C-positive inclusions), and ubiquitinated TDP-43-positive cytoplasmic inclusions in >95% of cases.

options.text: Selective destruction of post-ganglionic sympathetic neurons within the intermediolateral cell column of the thoracic cord
options.explanation: Intermediolateral cell column degeneration occurs in multiple system atrophy (Shy-Drager), causing severe orthostatic hypotension and autonomic failure, spared in ALS.

options.text: Demyelinating plaques confined to the periventricular white matter with prominent axonal preservation
options.explanation: Periventricular demyelinating plaques define multiple sclerosis, presenting with relapsing-remitting sensory, visual, and motor symptoms in young adults.
